title: Value-led pricing anchors: token qualifiers & tier guidance
content:
Executive summary:

This is a working note proposing a value-led framing for our pricing and packaging that keeps token-based metering as the primary usage metric but reframes how we talk about "tokens" to customers. The goal is to make the metric intuitive to product and finance buyers, reduce objection friction from enterprise procurement, and provide clear guardrails for tiered offers and discounts.

High-level thesis and user problem:
- Engineers and product teams care about predictability (latency + cost), control (model/versioning, deployment mode) and simplicity (clear unit economics).
- Finance and procurement care about unit cost, discounts tied to commitment, and ease-of-forecasting.
- Token pricing is the most accurate proxy for compute/quality delivered, but the term 'token' is opaque to many commercial buyers.

Positioning pillars (how we talk about it):
1) "Unit of delivered experience" — translate tokens into experience units buyers understand: "responses per minute at X quality tier" or "monthly active users at typical session length".
2) "Cost predictability controls" — emphasize knobs (reserved capacity, burst pools, soft limits, token caps) that convert the metered model into predictable spend.
3) "Layered commitments" — combine per-token usage billing with optional reserved capacity (Dedicated) and prebuy credits for discounts.
4) "Alignment to outcomes, not infrastructure" — show examples: support bot cost to serve 1M messages/month vs. recommendation batch embed cost per 100k rows.

Why keep token pricing (talk track):
- Accuracy: Tokens map closely to compute and memory (KV cache pressure), so unit prices reflect underlying costs across models and quantizations.
- Interoperability: Token metering works across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments without changing the billing primitive.
- Incentivizes efficiency: Customers gain meaningful levers (prompt engineering, caching, quantization) to reduce costs because savings are visible at token granularity.
- Simplicity at scale: One unit to measure usage across generations, embeddings, reranking and non-chat workloads.

Reframing tokens for buyers (recommended language):
- Use "Request Credits" or "Response Credits" as the external-facing unit in pricing pages and contract summaries (internal billing still token-based).
- Provide intuitive examples: "1,000 Response Credits ≈ 10k short-text completions; 100 credits ≈ 1 embedding (128-d)".
- Offer a credits calculator in console (estimate monthly spend by workload patterns).

Token qualifiers (new concept to clarify pricing signals):
Introduce short qualifiers that convey the major cost drivers without surfacing low-level infrastructure details: 
- "length factor" — average generation length per response
- "quality tier" — maps to model family (base, enhanced, high-accuracy)
- "interaction pattern" — streaming vs. single-shot vs. retrieval-heavy
These qualifiers let us show customers how their usage mixes change effective price per response.

Tier architecture (proposal):
- Dev (Free / Freemium): low monthly credits, API keys rate-limited, ideal for proof-of-concept.
- Growth: pay-as-you-go token credits, web console, basic analytics, community support.
- Production: volume discounts, token price reductions via commit, reserved burst capacity, per-route quotas and SLA.
- Enterprise (Dedicated / Private): blended pricing — base platform fee + discounted token rate + optional reserved GPU pools. Includes enterprise features (SAML, KMS, audit logs, extended retention).

Concrete discounting guardrails: (very opinionated)
- Volume bands for standard hosted token pricing: 0–100k credits = list price; 100k–1M = 10% off; 1M–5M = 20% off; 5M+ = negotiate (tiered/systematic).
- Commitment discounts (reserved credits or monthly committed spend): 6–12% for 6mo commit; 12–18% for 12mo; ensure minimum ARR thresholds to qualify for deeper discounts.
- Dedicated/Private: Offer a guaranteed performance SLA and invoice as a combination of 1) platform fee (annual) and 2) discounted token rate. Discounts scale with contract length and committed throughput (qps or reserved GPUs).
- No automatic additive stacking: Choose the best discount path (volume vs commit) and disallow simple stacking to keep math straightforward.

Sales & marketing talk tracks (short bullets):
- To developers: "Pay only for what you use; tokens = the work we do for you. Free tier and cost estimator in console."
- To product managers: "Predictability via reservations — convert variable usage into a committed, lower per-unit price."
- To finance: "Token billing + reserved capacity gives you both usage transparency and the ability to purchase predictable capacity with discounts. We provide monthly spend forecasts and alerting."
- To exec buyers: "We price for usage, not per-seat. If you run mission-critical workloads, Dedicated + reserved credits simplifies cost planning and unlocks our best pricing."

Competitive notes (quick scan):
- Vendor A (API-first) — very simple per-request pricing. Advantage: easy to explain. Drawback: hides variance by not exposing compute fidelity; harder to map to multiform workloads.
- Vendor B (instance-based) — charges by reserved endpoint/hour. Advantage: predictable; but forces overprovisioning and is inflexible for highly variable workloads.
- Our angle: hybrid — per-token clarity with reserved constructs to convert to predictable economics.

Sample site copy (short form):
- Headline: "Pay for outcomes, not hardware."
- Subhead: "Token-based metering that maps to real application cost—plus reservations to make spend predictable."
- CTA microcopy: "Estimate my monthly cost" -> launches calculator with recommended tier.

Sales-facing cheat sheet (one-pagers we should give AEs):
- How to explain tokens in 30s: analogize to "API calls" but adjusted for length/quality: "A short chat reply is fewer credits than a long multi-paragraph answer. Embeddings use a different credit rate because they are batched/optimized."
- Objection: "Tokens are opaque" -> Answer: "We translate tokens into concrete examples. We'll run a sample trace against your prompts to show likely spend and recommended reservations."
- Objection: "We need fixed cost" -> Answer: "Reserved capacity + monthly commitments convert metered spend into a fixed predictable payment with discounts."

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need a short name for the external-facing unit: Response Credits vs Request Credits vs Compute Credits — pick one and standardize across docs. (action: decide by 2025-10-15)
- Calculate realistic example mappings for common workloads (support chat, search relevance, embeddings at scale). Engineering to provide per-token cost multipliers for popular models (action: @Mateo).
- Design console estimator UX and integrate into signup flow (action: product + devex).
- Legal/Finance: draft contract language for reserved credits expiration, rollover, and refund policies. (action: Priya).

Appendix: example customer scenarios (brief)
- Scenario A — SMB support bot: 200k messages/month, avg 25 tokens/response. Recommendation: Growth tier with 200k credit prebuy -> 8–12% discount; enable KV caching and short-context prompts to reduce length factor.
- Scenario B — Marketplace product descriptions: 50k batch generation jobs, average 400 tokens/gen. Recommendation: Purchase Production tier; model selection to cheaper base family + enable batch parallelism; consider Dedicated for predictable latency if heavy throughput.

Notes to self (raw brainstorm):
- Could we expose per-route economics in the billing UI? Useful for customer value metrics and for suggesting targeted optimizations.
- Consider a promo: free reserved credits for 3 months if customer signs 12mo dedicated contract (pilot economics).
- Keep marketing site examples very concrete: "Generate 100k short chat replies for $X/mo" beats abstract credits.

References & links:
- Pricing framework doc (internal) — linked above
- Sample calculators + spreadsheet (WIP) — attach to PR when ready

End of draft.

Questions for reviewers:
1) Are volume band breakpoints reasonable? Any edge-cases from channel partners we should consider?
2) Acceptable external unit name? If you prefer a different term, list alternatives.
3) Any legal flags on reserved credit expiration rules?

-- Claire
